book: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology, 4th ed. (Rizzo)
kicker: Lesson 13 of your course, built from Chapter 13 of your Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology textbook (Rizzo). Test practice uses checked answers, because there is no official key for this test.

steps.title: What blood is made of
teach: Blood is a specialized connective tissue with two parts: the formed elements (blood cells) and the fluid plasma.
Plasma is about 55% of blood; the formed elements are about 45%. Women have about 5 liters of blood and men about 6. Blood is about 8% of body weight.

The formed elements are erythrocytes (red blood cells), leukocytes (white blood cells) and thrombocytes (platelets). Red blood cells are about 95% of the volume of blood cells. There are 700 times more red cells than white cells.

act.prompt: About what percentage of blood is plasma?
act.explanation: Plasma is about 55% of blood; the formed elements make up about 45%.

steps.title: What blood does
teach: Blood transports oxygen to cells and carbon dioxide to the lungs; carries nutrients, water and ions from the gut and wastes to the kidneys and sweat glands; and carries hormones and enzymes.
It regulates pH with buffers; normal blood pH is slightly basic at 7.35 to 7.45. Its water helps control body temperature, and its sodium helps control water in cells.
It prevents fluid loss by clotting, and protects against microbes and toxins with leukocytes.

act.prompt: What is the normal pH of blood?

steps.title: Plasma
teach: Plasma is 91% water. About 7% is protein: albumin (keeps osmotic pressure and water balance), globulins (antibodies, complement and transport molecules) and fibrinogen (needed for clotting). The last 2% is ions, nutrients, wastes, gases, enzymes and hormones.
Serum is plasma without the clotting factors: the clear yellow liquid left after blood clots.
Dr. Charles Drew developed blood storage methods that led to the first blood banks and directed the first American Red Cross blood bank.

act.prompt: Match each plasma protein to its job.

steps.title: Making blood cells
teach: Making blood cells is hematopoiesis. It happens in red bone marrow (myeloid tissue). The spleen, tonsils and lymph nodes also help make lymphocytes and monocytes.

All blood cells come from stem cells called hematocytoblasts. Some become red cells (losing their nuclei), some become the granular white cells, some become lymphocytes or monocytes, and megakaryoblasts become megakaryocytes, which break up into platelets.

steps.title: Red blood cells and hemoglobin
teach: Erythrocytes are biconcave disks with no nucleus, so they can’t divide. They last about 120 days.

Hemoglobin makes up about a third (33%) of the cell’s volume. It has two parts: heme, a pigment with four iron atoms that bind oxygen in the lungs, and globin, a protein that carries carbon dioxide back to the lungs.
Oxygen-carrying hemoglobin is bright red; without oxygen it’s darker red. Men have about 5.4 million red cells per cubic millimeter, women about 4.8 million. Iron in the diet supports hemoglobin.

steps.title: White blood cells
teach: Leukocytes have nuclei and no pigment. They fight inflammation and infection, move into tissues by ameboid movement and eat debris and microbes by phagocytosis. There are 5,000 to 9,000 per cubic millimeter.
Granular leukocytes (granules show with Wright’s stain): neutrophils (60% to 70%, the most numerous), eosinophils (2% to 4%) and basophils (0.5% to 1%).
Agranular leukocytes: monocytes (3% to 8%) and lymphocytes (20% to 25%).

mnemonic.explanation: Neutrophils, Lymphocytes, Monocytes, Eosinophils, Basophils: most to least common.

steps.title: What each white blood cell does
teach: Neutrophils are the most common and respond first to bacteria; they make lysozyme. Pus is largely dead neutrophils.
Monocytes are the largest; they become macrophages in tissues and eat bacteria and debris.
Eosinophils fight allergy triggers (pollen, cat hair), make antihistamines and attack some worm parasites.
Basophils join allergic reactions and secrete heparin (anticoagulant), histamine (inflammatory) and serotonin (vasoconstrictor).
Lymphocytes are the smallest; they make antibodies and drive the immune response (B and T cells).

steps.title: Platelets
teach: Thrombocytes, or platelets, are tiny disk-shaped cell fragments (2 to 4 micrometers) made from megakaryocytes in red marrow. They live about a week.
They start the chain of reactions that clots blood when a vessel is damaged.

steps.title: How blood clots
teach: Small damaged vessels constrict. In larger ones, clotting (coagulation) takes over in three stages.

Stage 1: platelets clump at the rough cut surface, and damaged tissue releases thromboplastin, leading to prothrombin activator (calcium needed). Stage 2: prothrombin activator, with calcium ions, converts prothrombin (made by the liver) into thrombin. Stage 3: thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads, which trap blood cells and platelets: the clot.
Clot retraction, or syneresis, tightens the clot. Serum is left behind. After repair, fibrinolysis dissolves the clot. Vitamin K is needed for many clotting factors.

act.prompt: Put the clotting steps in order.

items.label: Platelets clump and thromboplastin is released

steps.title: Unwanted clots
teach: Plaque, a cholesterol-containing mass, roughens a vessel wall and can start clotting where it isn’t needed.

Thrombosis is clotting in an unbroken vessel; the clot is a thrombus. A piece that breaks off and travels in the blood is an embolus; when it lodges and blocks a vessel, that’s an embolism. Tissue killed by lost blood supply is an infarction.
Exercise helps prevent unwanted clots; smoking increases fibrinogen and raises the risk.

steps.title: ABO blood groups
teach: Mismatched blood causes agglutination, the clumping of red cells: a transfusion reaction between plasma antibodies and red cell antigens.

Type A has antigen A and anti-B antibodies. Type B has antigen B and anti-A. Type AB has both antigens and no antibodies: the universal recipient. Type O has neither antigen and both antibodies: the universal donor.

steps.title: The Rh blood group
teach: The Rh group is named after Rhesus monkeys, where antigen D was first identified and studied. Red cells with antigen D are Rh positive (most Americans); without it, Rh negative.
Anti-Rh antibodies form only after an Rh-negative person is exposed to Rh-positive blood. A second exposure causes agglutination.
An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive baby can become sensitized; in later pregnancies her antibodies can destroy the baby’s red cells (erythroblastosis fetalis). RhoGAM prevents this.

act.prompt: Which antigen was first identified in the Rh group?

options.label: A
options.feedback: A belongs to the ABO group.

options.label: O
options.feedback: Type O means no A or B antigen.

steps.title: Blood disorders
teach: Anemia means the blood carries too little oxygen. Sickle-cell anemia: inherited; red blood cells (erythrocytes) are sickle-shaped with abnormal hemoglobin. Hemolytic anemia: red cells rupture or are destroyed faster than normal. Thalassemia: inherited; hemoglobin production is suppressed. Iron-deficiency anemia: low red cell production.

Hemophilia: an inherited clotting disorder from a recessive gene on the X chromosome. Thrombocytopenia: a serious drop in platelets. Erythrocytosis (polycythemia): too many red cells. Leukemia: cancer with abnormal white cell production.
Septicemia is blood poisoning from microbes and toxins. Malaria is a parasite in red cells spread by mosquitoes. Mononucleosis is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus.

items.label: Recessive gene on the X chromosome

steps.title: Blood and aging
teach: Before birth, blood cells are made in the spleen, liver and yolk sac; by the third trimester the red marrow takes over.

Smoking adds carbon monoxide, which binds hemoglobin (carboxyhemoglobin) and reduces oxygen transport. Long antibiotic courses can kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K and cause bleeding problems. Anemias, clotting problems and chronic leukemias become more common with age.

options.label: It binds to hemoglobin and blocks oxygen transport
It thins the blood
options.feedback: It stops red cells from carrying oxygen.

quiz.q: The most numerous white blood cell type are the __________________, which comprise 60–70% of all white blood cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says neutrophils make up 60% to 70% of white blood cells, the most common leukocytes. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Heparin, histamine, and serotonin are secreted by______________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says basophils release heparin, histamine and serotonin into tissues. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: A piece of a blood clot that dislodges and is transported by the bloodstream is called a(n) _________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says a piece of a blood clot that dislodges and is transported by the bloodstream is an embolus. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: White blood cells as a group are called ____________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says white blood cells are leukocytes. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Agglutination of RBCs is the result of a transfusion reaction caused by _____________________ blood.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says agglutination is the result of a transfusion reaction caused by mismatched blood. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Hematopoiesis occurs in the __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says hematopoiesis occurs in red bone marrow. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Chemical secretions from __________________________ attack some worm parasites in the body.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says the chemical secretions of eosinophils attack some worm parasites. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Prothrombin activator, with the assistance of ______________ ions, converts prothrombin to thrombin.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says prothrombin activator, in the presence of calcium ions, converts prothrombin into thrombin. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Red blood cells make up about _______ % of the volume of blood cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says erythrocytes make up about 95% of the volume of blood cells. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Antibodies are produced by __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says lymphocytes are involved in the production of antibodies. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: A cholesterol-containing mass that adheres to the smooth walls of blood vessels is called a(n) __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says a cholesterol-containing mass that adheres to the walls of blood vessels is called plaque. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Blood poisoning is also known as __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says septicemia is also known as blood poisoning. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: An example of an agranular leukocyte is a(n) __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 lists monocytes and lymphocytes as the agranular leukocytes. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: The Rh blood group consists of those individuals with the ___ antigen, the first identified and studied.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says antigen D was the first Rh antigen identified and studied. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Blood plasma without clotting factors is called __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says serum is blood plasma without the clotting factors. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: After _______________ leave the blood and enter tissues, they increase in size and are called macrophages.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says monocytes increase in size after entering tissues and are then called macrophages. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: An excessive amount of red blood cells can cause __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says erythrocytosis is caused by an excessive amount of red blood cells. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Clot retraction is called __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says clot retraction is called syneresis. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Clotting in an unbroken blood vessel is called __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says clotting in an unbroken vessel is called thrombosis. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Megakaryoblasts mature into __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says megakaryoblasts mature into blood platelets. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: An inherited form of anemia in which erythrocytes rupture or are destroyed at a faster rate than normal is known as __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says hemolytic anemia is an inherited condition in which erythrocytes rupture or are destroyed faster than normal. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Approximately one third of the erythrocyte cell volume is composed of ________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says hemoglobin constitutes 33% of the red blood cell’s volume. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Smoking increases __________________________ levels in the blood, thus increasing the possibility of unwanted clotting.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says smoking increases fibrinogen levels in the blood, increasing the possibility of unwanted clotting. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: The serious decrease in the number of thrombocytes or blood platelets is a condition known as __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says thrombocytopenia is a serious decrease in the number of platelets. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: The genetically inherited clotting disorder __________________________ is associated with the expression of a recessive gene on the X chromosome.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says hemophilia is an inherited clotting disorder associated with a recessive gene on the X chromosome. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Plasma accounts for about 55% of blood.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says plasma accounts for about 55% of blood. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: The normal pH of blood is at 7.35 to 7.45.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says the normal pH of blood is 7.35 to 7.45. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Sickle-cell anemia is a hereditary disease in which leukocytes have an abnormal sickle shape due to abnormal hemoglobin.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. In sickle-cell anemia it’s the erythrocytes (red blood cells), not leukocytes, that are sickle-shaped. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Hemoglobin has five iron atoms that combine with oxygen gas in the lungs.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 13 says heme contains four iron atoms, not five. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.

quiz.q: Thrombin forms the threads of a blood clot, which enmesh the blood cells and platelets seeping from the wound.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Fibrin forms the threads of the clot. Thrombin is the enzyme that converts fibrinogen into fibrin. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 13.
